data.title: ICE officer pleads not guilty to lying to FBI about Minneapolis shooting
data.description:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer pleaded not guilty Friday to federal charges stemming from allegations that he lied to authorities about what led up to the January shooting of a Venezuelan man during Minneapolis enforcement operations.

A federal grand jury indicted Christian Castro, 52, in early September on six counts of making materially false statements to investigators. He appeared before a magistrate judge in St. Paul on Friday where he was arraigned on the charges.

Castro, who has reportedly been suspended without pay from the agency, is the first federal immigration officer to be prosecuted by the Justice Department for actions that occurred during Operation Metro Surge in the Twin Cities.

“Mr. Castro voluntarily went to Minneapolis to surrender himself, both in state court and in federal court, and he’s been released on bond, and we look forward to litigating these matters and to presenting our case in court and exonerating him,” Michael Wynn, one of his attorneys, told The Hill.

Castro is accused of lying to the FBI about how a Jan. 14 scuffle with three men, one of whom was shot in the thigh and hospitalized, unfolded.

Officials with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) initially claimed that an officer, determined to be Castro, fired a “defensive shot” after being attacked with a snow shovel and a broom handle. But court documents indicated that the men had actually dropped the items and ran toward a nearby apartment “as soon as [they] saw his pistol.”

About a month later, DHS said they were investigating what appeared to be “untruthful statements” made by the officer following the review of additional video evidence.

“The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct. Violations of this sacred sworn oath will not be tolerated,” a former spokesperson said at the time.

Friday’s hearing caps off what has been a chaotic few weeks for Castro, who became the center of an extradition fight between Texas Gov. Abbott (R) and Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz (D) after he was jailed in Texas in late May.

Walz accused his counterpart of delay and refusal to sign the paperwork that would have authorized Castro’s transfer so he could face state assault charges in connection with the shooting. A federal judge ultimately declined to intervene, and Castro was released after 90 days.

He was arrested again on Wednesday by Minnesota authorities and made his initial appearance in a state courtroom the next day.

He is currently required to wear a GPS ankle monitor and cannot possess any firearms as part of his bond conditions in the federal case.

data.title: Congress can come together to honor the Adams Family
data.description:
There is plenty that Republicans and Democrats disagree about in Washington. Honoring the extraordinary contributions of the Adams family to the United States should not be one of them.

As the four members of the House of Representatives serving on the Adams Memorial Commission, we represent different parts of the country, different parties, and different political perspectives. But we are united in the belief that John Adams, Abigail Adams, John Quincy Adams, and their remarkable family deserve a permanent memorial in our nation’s capital.

Few American families have contributed as much to the founding, development and preservation of the nation.

John Adams was a leading voice for American independence, a signer of the Declaration of Independence, a diplomat who helped negotiate America’s first international alliance to secure critical financial and military support for the Revolution, and, ultimately, the second president of the United States.

His wife, Abigail, was far more than a witness to that history. During long periods when John was serving the country at home and abroad, she managed their family and farm while becoming one of his most trusted political advisers. Her remarkable correspondence provides an enduring account of the founding era, including her famous appeal to “remember the ladies” at a time when women possessed few political or legal rights.

Their son, John Quincy, carried that tradition of public service into another generation. He served as a diplomat, secretary of State, and the sixth president before returning to public service in the House of Representatives, where he became a fierce opponent of slavery.

And those three lives barely scratch the surface of the Adams family’s contributions to the United States. The family produced generations of diplomats, public servants, writers, and civic leaders whose influence extended far beyond the founding era.

Yet there is still no memorial in Washington honoring this extraordinary American family.

That omission is especially striking as Americans commemorate the 250th anniversary of our independence. John Adams helped make that independence possible. Abigail Adams helped give voice to the principles the new nation would spend generations working to fulfill. Their descendants demonstrated how the responsibilities of citizenship and public service could be passed from one generation to the next.

A memorial to the Adams family would be different from the monuments Washington already knows so well. It would not commemorate only a president, general, or individual achievement. It would tell the story of an American family — men and women, parents and children — bound together across generations by a commitment to public service. The current proposal envisions that memorial near the White House, where John and Abigail became its first residents in 1800.

At a time when Americans hear so much about what divides us, the Adams Memorial offers a small but meaningful reminder of what can still unite us. Republicans and Democrats in the House have already come together unanimously behind this effort.

The Adams family gave generations of service to the country they helped create. Two hundred and fifty years after the Declaration of Independence, it is time for our nation’s capital to give them the recognition they deserve.

The Senate should pass the Adams Memorial-Great American Heroes Act and help make that memorial a reality.

Morgan Griffith, William R. Keating, Stephen F. Lynch and John Moolenaar serve as commissioners on the Adams Memorial Commission.

data.title: JFK's family slams Trump over Kennedy Center: 'How small minded, how narcissistic'
data.description:
The family of former President John F. Kennedy slammed President Trump for his ongoing legal battle to put his name on the Kennedy Center and to close the building planned renovations.

The Kennedy Center board, handpicked by Trump, voted Tuesday to close the main building, but Trump said the renovations will not happen as long as the ruling blocking his name from being added to the center stands.

“If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

JFK’s niece Maria Shriver, who was the former first lady of California, said Trump’s statement “blows my mind,” calling the president “small minded” and “narcissistic.”

“That a sitting president would not let any renovations to a public building go on unless he gets to first put his name in the said building… What a sad state of affairs. What a tragedy,” she wrote on the social platform X.

“It seems that this man will not rest until his name is permanently connected to the name of a great president, whose memory this building was dedicated to,” she added.

JFK’s grandson Jack Schlossberg, who recently ran an unsuccessful campaign in New York’s 12th Congressional District, also weighed in.

“JFK’s legacy is unbreakable — the moon, the Civil Rights Act, Cuban Missile Crisis and the arts. Trump is a broken band in nose dive decline,” he said in a statement.

Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex-officio board member, sued in December to block the name change and closure plans. U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled against the board and blocked its attempt to add Trump’s name to the building’s facade.

Kerry Kennedy, the daughter of former Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy, called Beatty a “national hero” for challenging the board and the administration in court.

“She has fiercely and courageously stood up for the Kennedy Center, for the arts, for Uncle Jack’s memory, for this country’s history, and most importantly, for the law, time and time again,” she wrote on social media. “We will not be bullied into silence or submission. Thank you, Rep. Beatty. We are all so grateful for your leadership.”

Her brother, Trump’s Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., has said in the past that he has “bigger fish to fry” than worrying about a name change.

data.title: Watch live: Vance takes Trump's midterm message to Iowa
data.description:
Vice President Vance is rallying voters in Iowa on Friday, as GOP candidates in the Hawkeye State navigate a complicated political landscape ahead of November.

The visit marks Vance’s second trip to the state this election cycle and as Republicans hope to maintain control of the House and Senate next year. GOP gubernatorial nominee Zach Lahn is expected to join him.

Notably, Senate nominee Rep. Ashley Hinson (R), who is running to replace outgoing Sen. Joni Ernst (R), is skipping the event. She recently broke with President Trump on his beef import plan while other Republicans in the state questioned the Trump administration over its Iran war strategy.

The event in Council Bluffs, Iowa, is set to begin at 1 p.m. EDT.

Watch the live video above.

data.title: Live updates: Vance stumps in Iowa as races tighten; Iran war's cost exceeds $43B
data.description:
The Midwest is home to several contentious congressional and gubernatorial races in November, historically red areas that are seeing Democratic candidates make inroads.

Vice President Vance is set to visit one of them for a rally on Friday: Council Bluffs, Iowa. He is expected to be joined by Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn, who is running against Democratic State Auditor Rob Sand.

The rally’s location is the turf of Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek, who is campaigning against Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) for the open seat. Hinson reportedly won’t attend the Vance event.

In Kansas, Adam Hamilton (D) narrowly leads Republican Sen. Roger Marshall in a tight race for Senate, according a The Hill/Emerson College poll out Friday. It found Hamilton ahead by 2 percentage points, with 45 percent support to Marshall’s 43 percent.

The Pentagon told congressional leaders this week that the cost of the Iran war through Sept. 3 had exceeded $43 billion, not including damage estimates to sites hit.

At the White House, President Trump will make an announcement about Medicaid drug prices on Friday afternoon. He’ll hold other meetings and will head Friday evening to his golf course in Sterling, Va., for a MAGA Inc. meeting. He’ll spend part of the weekend at Camp David.

Follow live below.

data.title: Supreme Court campaign ruling puts insiders and party bosses over everyday people
data.description:
Statewide elections in North Carolina are highly competitive and extremely expensive. Voters make it the country’s ultimate swing state, having voted for President Trump and for me in 2016 and 2020. That also makes it a top target for Washington insiders and big money interests who try to buy elections for their favorite candidates.

When I announced my candidacy for Senate, we already knew big money would play an oversized role in trying to keep this seat in Republican hands. Although polls have had my campaign ahead, we always knew the race would be close. Democrats running for Senate in North Carolina often seem like they’re winning in the summer only to get their hearts broken in the fall. Our last Democratic senator was elected almost two decades ago and we have only elected two Democrats in almost 40 years.

Many people look at the polls along with the unpopular actions coming out of Washington and think we have this race won already. Instead of working to lower prices and deliver for working families like they promised, President Trump has insisted on his costly tariffs while he and his allies have dragged our country into an unpopular, chaotic and endless war, while the cost of gas, groceries, utilities and health care have all spiked.

But they just might get away with these failings because Republicans in Washington have another card up their sleeves for the midterms: their massive, multi-million dollar war chests.

Instead of doing what leaders should do and deliver results, Republicans have tossed out the rulebook and handed billionaires and special interests even more influence over our elections. This tactic upends my campaign and other close races by further silencing the voices of everyday people in favor of big money and national party committees.

It started last month with the Supreme Court’s worst campaign finance decision since Citizens United. In NRSC v. FEC, the Supreme Court removed coordination limits, giving parties and political committees, which raise money at one hundred times the limits of campaigns, the ability to spend virtually unlimited amounts of money on advertising.

This decision is uniquely painful in North Carolina. My opponent is Michael Whatley, former chair of the Republican National Committee, who spent his career lobbying for Big Oil and utility companies as they raised prices and rates on families. The ruling uniquely helps candidates like him. His elite DC connections have already resulted in an onslaught of tens of millions of dollars in ads on the airwaves.

Then, in yet another emergency Supreme Court ruling — after ballots were mailed — Trump’s FCC allies completed their scheme at the Supreme Court. Upending decades of law, the court allowed the FCC to require local television broadcasters to give these same coordinated party committees a massive discount on television ads.

Now, they can not only spend unlimited amounts, but they can also do it at discount rates. The law clearly states that only candidate committees should get these rates as they are bound by much stricter campaign limits. But just like Trump’s White House Ballroom case, the court let Republicans off the hook on a technicality — not on the law.

This means the Republican National Committee, in coordination with their old boss Michael Whatley, can now buy four, five, or in some cases as many as 16 ads for the price they paid for one ad in 2024. That is a massive, legally mandated corporate-funded discount.

This is one big recipe for the wealthiest and well-connected to bail out their favored candidates. When you’re running to have the backs of everyday people, the big corporate interests tend to set their sights on defeating you.

As the former party chair running in the most competitive Senate race in the country, in one of the most expensive states to communicate, Michael Whatley is perfectly positioned to benefit from the Republican National Committee’s $130 million dollar war chest.

Life is really hard for working families right now. Everything is more expensive, from gas, to groceries to health care. I’m running to Make Stuff Cost Less. But, as Washington Republicans flood North Carolina with hundreds of millions of dollars of lies, they are banking on the fact that they can drown out that message.

I am a prisoner of hope. I truly believe our best days are ahead of us. But Washington is broken, and instead of trying to fix it, they are trying to rig the game in their favor. Enough is enough. Washington needs some North Carolina common sense.

Roy Cooper served as governor of North Carolina from 2017-2025. He is the state’s Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate.

data.title: Where Trump's hunting, fishing order will have the most impact
data.description:
President Trump on Thursday signed new executive orders aimed at expanding hunting and fishing access in the U.S., rolling back restrictions on these activities. 

The president unveiled “Reinvigorating America’s Hunting Heritage” and “Restoring American Saltwater Angling and Recreation” during a Thursday White House Rose Garden dinner with over 100 hunters, anglers and outdoor officials. 

“We believe that public lands belong to the American people and to the public, and hunters, fishers, and outdoorsmen should be able to access them,” Trump said. 

Here’s what you need to know about where these orders will have the most impact: 

What lands will open up?

Under the hunting executive order, Trump directed Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to reverse “years of overregulation” under previous administrations and expand hunting access on some federal lands. 

This is an expansion upon the Trump administration’s August order, which opened up over 92 million acres across 32 states for hunting. 

The new order directs Burgum to permit hunting within 90 days of its signing in California’s Castle Mountains National Monument and within Idaho’s Craters of the Moon National Monument.

The California monument protects almost 21,000 acres of land in the Mojave Desert near Nevada. Craters of the Moon National Monument is in the south-central region of Idaho between Boise and Yellowstone National Park and features a 618 square-mile lava field.

Trump’s order restricts hunting on these federal lands only for species that are not protected under 16 U.S.C. 1533 of the U.S. Endangered Species Act. 

“I have determined that appropriately managed hunting would not put the objects of historic and scientific interest that these monuments protect at risk,” the president wrote in his executive order. 

Rolling back Biden-era lead rules 

The president directed his administration to authorize the use of traditional lead ammunition and tackle within 180 days of this order. 

Under former President Biden, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Administration in 2023 expanded a ban on the use of lead tackle and ammunition in eight national wildlife refuges to safeguard these areas from potential lead poisoning risks. 

Republican lawmakers and hunters have pushed back against these restrictions, citing increased costs associated with alternatives to lead products. 

“Lead ammunition was a problem, huh? Is it better than other ammunition? I assume, huh? That’s pretty good,” Trump told the crowd at the Thursday Rose Garden event. 

“I don’t know what the hell that means, but I know one thing: You wanted it,” he continued. “You wanted it, and I’m here for you.” 

Promotes Sunday hunting on federal lands

The hunting order also instructs Burgum to encourage states to “promote and expand” Sunday hunting on state and federal lands within a year of its signing. 

Burgum touted these new initiatives in a social media post Thursday, saying the Trump administration is committed to “putting American hunters, fishermen and outdoorsmen FIRST.”

“Sportsmen are among our greatest conservationists, and this administration is committed to supporting the men and women who help protect our public lands and wildlife,” the secretary wrote.

data.title: 25 years later, President Trump has discarded the lessons of 9/11
data.description:
After the horrific assault on our country on Sept. 11, 2001, Congress came together to confront the failures that left our nation vulnerable and build a stronger homeland security system to prevent another attack. During his second term, President Donald Trump has dismantled and politicized our national security programs and federal law enforcement to such a degree that he is leaving us vulnerable to another large-scale terrorist attack. At the same time, he has recklessly launched an illegal and failing war in Iran — drastically increasing threats to the nation.

As leaders in Congress who have overseen — and helped create — many of our national security programs over the past 25 years, we know we need to focus on plugging real security gaps — not senselessly creating new ones while turning agencies created to protect us against the American people.

After 9/11, Congress, with bipartisan support, created anti-terrorism grants to help cities and states protect themselves from future attacks. Yet the Trump administration has wasted time and resources by making these critical grants the subject of political handwringing and litigation, while withholding, reducing or delaying hundreds of millions of dollars in security funding for our communities.

For example, the Trump administration attempted to cut New York state and New York City’s grant funding last year by $187 million and only retreated after political blowback and lawsuits — some of which are ongoing. It is an outrage that anti-terrorism grant money rightfully owed to our brave first responders, is now something communities must fight for in court.

Twenty-five years after terrorists defeated a weak aviation security system to carry out the deadliest-ever attack on U.S. soil, the Trump administration is pushing to bring back that same flawed system by moving to privatize the Transportation Security Administration — an idea straight out of Project 2025. If our aviation security is privatized, security contractors would undoubtedly carve out profits by cutting elsewhere. Going back to the pre-9/11 model would lead to weaknesses in security screening — putting traveling Americans at risk solely so corporations could make a profit.

Trump has also gone after the counterterrorism and intelligence workforces within the Department of Homeland Security, the FBI and the National Counterterrorism Center. When Democrats took control of Congress in 2007, we both worked to ensure passage of the Implementing Recommendations of the 9/11 Commission Act as one of our first acts, which, together with other reforms, mandated the integration of intelligence and bolstered information sharing across federal agencies. Trump’s purging of patriotic, career employees at these agencies has not only cost the United States deep institutional knowledge built over decades, but it has also damaged our international partnerships. Our allies are increasingly nervous about sharing information with us as Trump alienates them and cozies up to Russia.

The 9/11 Commission Report concluded that before 9/11, the U.S. government’s “most important failure was one of imagination.”

Now, with repeated warnings from the intelligence community and cybersecurity experts about China’s increased cyber capabilities and the potential cyber risks of advanced artificial intelligence, it should not be difficult for the Trump administration to imagine the growing threat of a significant cyberattack. Instead of working to prevent such an attack, Trump pushed out a third of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s staff and cut cybersecurity personnel across the federal government.

Now, with China pre-positioning on critical infrastructure networks, Iran hacking water utilities across the country, and new AI cyber risks being announced regularly, we are left with a weakened federal government that lacks the expertise and resources necessary to keep us secure in cyberspace.

Trump’s unnecessary war with Iran is making us less safe at home, too. Americans have been under a heightened threat environment since Trump picked a fight with Iran, the leading state sponsor of terrorism and a country that Trump’s National Counterterrorism Center Director said, “posed no imminent threat.” By July, the State Department had issued a rare warning to all Americans that they could be targeted while abroad. This is in addition to Iran already attempting to attack our critical infrastructure that Americans rely on every day.

We’ve seen our adversaries engaging in more brazen behavior as they clearly want to see our country weakened. And, outrageously, they see Trump doing their work for them. They see the administration’s tunnel vision with Trump’s obsession with his mass deportation agenda. He has diverted thousands of law enforcement personnel from their normal duties, such as preventing terrorism and stopping terrorism financing, to instead carry out drastic immigration sweeps. Trump has also undone the work of the Justice Department and FBI to enforce our laws and prosecute violence. We can’t forget that our adversaries see that Trump has already let extremists who launched an attack on our democracy off the hook, pardoning over 1,500 involved in the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol.

Instead of strengthening our efforts to stop America’s adversaries from conducting attacks on our country, President Trump is opening the door to potential new attacks by creating security gaps in almost every area of national security. With Republicans in charge of Congress unwilling — or unable — to stop Trump from weakening the nation, Democrats must be prepared to lead, hold this administration accountable for the damage it has done, and rebuild the homeland security apparatus so it protects Americans from terror threats while preserving Americans’ constitutional rights.

It is essential that our Republican colleagues wake up to the risks we face before it’s too late.

Nancy Pelosi represents the 11th District of California and is a former House Speaker. Bennie Thompson represents Mississippi’s 2nd District and is ranking member of the Homeland Security Committee.

data.title: More than 100 Democratic operatives urge party leaders to reject AI cash
data.description:
More than 170 Democratic organizers and campaign staff members are calling on the party’s leaders to reject campaign donations from the pro-artificial intelligence super PAC Leading the Future (LTF) as the debate over AI safety and regulations intensifies in Washington.

The letter, first shared with The Hill on Friday, argues the millions of dollars from AI industry executives is “fundamentally at odds with the Democratic Party’s core values.”

“We are a party that values people over unchecked regressive power, that believes in the role of government in reining in corporate greed and that advocates for accountability and fairness in our economy,” the letter states.

Leading the Future is at the center of the AI industry’s campaign spending push. It has received millions from OpenAI President Greg Brockman, the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, AI firm Perplexity and venture capitalist Joe Lonsdale. 

Ezra Andres-Tysch, a Democratic strategist who helped organize the letter, said he hopes the letter “makes it easier for someone to go to their their campaign manager or their candidate and say, why are we doing this?”

“Why are we, you know, taking money from these campaigns? Why are we holding these positions that aren’t popular?” he added.

“One of the reasons that I hope that this kind of breaks through is often campaign staff are that connection line to a candidate,” Andres-Tysch told The Hill. “I think often candidates live in their own little worlds, and then the campaign staff who are knocking on doors, talking to real people, can be that canary in a coal mine.”

It comes as concerns mount over the future of AI development and its potential impacts on jobs, the environment and national security. Earlier this week, more than a dozen Democratic congressional candidates started a new push to call on campaigns to refuse LTF’s money.

LTF has raised at least $140 million for the 2026 midterm election cycle. The spending group has donated to members on both sides of the aisle, maintaining its goal to “support a well-balanced, cross-partisan conversation about artificial intelligence.”

This “starts with passing a strong and thoughtful national regulatory framework,” the super PAC said in a statement earlier this year. “Our north star is to support a political environment where policymakers at the federal and state levels can tune out the extremes and engage thoughtfully on critical policy issues surrounding innovation in and adoption of AI.”

The super PAC says a framework should include safety protections for kids, baseline safety standards for frontier models, and commitments around AI literary and workforce training.

Following an AI researcher’s ominous warning about the technology, lawmakers in Washington scrambled this week to manage the abrupt panic around AI development, floating numerous proposals to prevent its negative potential.

Strategists in the Friday letter argued the technology “poses extreme risks to the public” and “requires clear guardrails to protect Americans and create accountability for tech companies that fail to adhere to basic guardrails.”

Commenting on past proposals, LTF said AI deserves “rigorous debate as Congress works toward durable solutions that protect the public while accelerating American innovation and leadership.”

data.title: Hollywood handouts shouldn't come before environmental cleanup
data.description:
Representatives from both parties are drafting a federal tax incentive for the movie industry — a move likely to give taxpayers a poor return on their money. New evidence highlights the type of spending that benefits communities one can overlook when jetting from Los Angeles to Gotham.

State and local governments have a history of throwing cash at firms to entice them to their jurisdiction. My review of credible studies regarding relocation incentives found that, on average, 93 percent of relocating firms would have come anyway. Incentives for Hollywood fit the pattern. An audit of Georgia’s Film Tax Credit found that for each dollar the state gave, 19 cents came back. Although tax revenue is just one metric, it shows the unfavorable deal taxpayers gave for Hollywood to come down to Georgia.

Governments at all levels should exit the business of ad-hoc corporate tax incentives and focus on what they are uniquely positioned to do: fund broadly enjoyed goods that others won’t. A prime example is funding the cleanup of environmental hazards that plague many communities and the restoration of the amenities they once enjoyed. A corporation can pocket a tax incentive and move on; no one can pocket a river made healthy for fish and people or a site suitable for new homes.

Abandoned mine drainage contaminates as many as 39,000 miles of streams in Appalachia alone. Interviews with residents of mine-affected areas reveal that mine-polluted waterways foster pessimism about the future and neglect in the present, with one type of pollution, mine drainage,  leading to others, trash dumping. People leave such places if they have the chance: from 1990 to 2020, Pennsylvania communities with mine drainage problems and no restoration saw their population decline by 9 percent. That’s almost 1 in 10 people moving elsewhere.

Supported by public funding, grassroots organizations have built and maintained hundreds of wetland systems to treat mine drainage, improving water clarity for miles downstream. Residents near restored waterways report a new sense of pride of place and optimism about the future. As a result, longtime residents stayed and new ones came, especially those with more education. 

The cost? About $240 per resident of a Census tract with restoration. By comparison, the federal Empowerment Zone program, which mainly consisted of business incentives, spent $1,500 per resident and attracted fewer people to select Census tracts.

Treating abandoned mine drainage is one of many possibilities for high-return public investments that cannot be uprooted and offshored. Brownfields are another. Remediating them — assuming no responsible party exists to do it — turns a community hazard into an asset for repurposing. 

An example is Pennsylvania’s Hazardous Sites Cleanup Act program, which helped turn the site of a former steel and coke plant in Pittsburgh into innovation centers and advanced manufacturing facilities. A study of brownfield cleanups showed that by increasing property values they would generate, with reassessments, enough tax revenue in one year to more than cover cleanup costs. Compare that to the Georgia film tax credit that repays 19 cents on the dollar.  

The bipartisan Ohio River Restoration Program Act, sponsored by Sens. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) and Todd Young (R-Ind.), aims to remediate toxic substances, protect drinking water sources, restore fish and wildlife habitat and create opportunities for public access and recreation. The act won’t produce Hollywood blockbusters, but its proposed funding is $350 million a year. 

Meanwhile, Los Angeles filmmakers flying over the Ohio Valley can tap New York’s film tax credits for up to $700 million a year.

Jeremy G. Weber is professor at the University of Pittsburgh School of Public and International Affairs and author of “Statistics for Public Policy: A Practical Guide to Being Mostly Right” (or at Least Respectably Wrong), University of Chicago Press.
